title: CHAPTER 3 International Political Economy (IPE)
content: ✨ እንኳን ወደ ሦስተኛው ምዕራፍ (Chapter 3) በሰላም መጣችሁ! በዚህ ክፍል ስለ International Political Economy (IPE) ምንነት፣ በState እና Market መካከል ስላለው ግንኙነት፣ የባህላዊ ብያኔዎች ውስንነት፣ እና የ GPE (Global Political Economy) መምጣት በጥልቀት እናያለን። ተከታተሉኝ👇👇 ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 📌 What is International Political Economy? At its core, International Political Economy (IPE) studies how political power and economic forces interact across national borders. It bridges the gap between politics (states, power, rules) and economics (markets, wealth, resource allocation). 📌 The Traditional State-vs-Market Definition & Its Limitations • The Traditional View: IPE is often defined as the study of the tension between the State (where individuals take collective action) and the Market (where self-interested individuals and firms operate). • Assumptions of this View: 1. There are only two major actors: States and Markets. 2. States and markets interact in a purely adversarial, opposing way. 💡 Key Analysis & Core Limitations: • Ignores Key Non-State Actors: It leaves out Transnational Corporations (TNCs/MNCs), international organizations, and global social movements that hold immense economic power. • Overlooks Cooperation: The state-market relationship is not always hostile. It is often cooperative, reciprocal, or mutually constitutive (markets need states to enforce laws, and states need markets to generate wealth). • Strict Borders: Traditional views assume a rigid boundary between internal (national) and external (international) affairs, which modern globalization has blurred. 📌 The Shift from IPE to Global Political Economy (GPE) Because large corporations operate across global production networks (designing, manufacturing, and marketing products across multiple countries), scholars increasingly use the term Global Political Economy (GPE) to reflect these borderless economic realities. 📌 A Broader, Comprehensive Definition of IPE To account for all dynamic actors, IPE is best defined as: "A field of inquiry that studies the ever-changing relationships between governments, businesses, and social forces across history and across geographical areas." 📌 The Two Core Dimensions of IPE: 1. The Political Dimension: • Deals with the use of power by states, international organizations, NGOs, and TNCs. • Focuses on decision-making regarding the allocation of tangible resources (money, products) and intangible assets (security, innovation, regulatory authority). 2. The Economic Dimension: • Deals with how scarce resources are distributed among individuals, groups, and nation-states. • Views the market not merely as a physical meeting place, but as a global driving force shaping human behavior, investment, and trade. 📝 Exam Hint: Exams often ask why traditional IPE definitions are insufficient. Remember to highlight that traditional definitions ignore TNCs/MNCs and treat state-market relationships purely as a tension, missing their cooperative nature. 👉 IPE ማለት በፖለቲካዊ ሥልጣን (State/Power) እና በኢኮኖሚያዊ ገበያ (Market/Wealth) መካከል ያለውን ግንኙነት የሚያጠና የትምህርት ዘርፍ ነው። የቀደሙት ብያኔዎች (Traditional Definitions) ትኩረት የሚያደርጉት በሀገር (State) እና በገበያ (Market) መካከል ባለው ግጭት ላይ ብቻ ነበር። ነገር ግን በዛሬው ዓለም እንደ TNCs/MNCs (ተሻጋሪ ኩባንያዎች) ያሉ ትልልቅ ተዋንያን ስላሉ፣ አዲሱ ብያኔ እነዚህን በሙሉ ያካተተ ሰፊ አስተሳሰብ (Global Political Economy) ይከተላል።

title: 3.2. Classical Theoretical Perspectives: Mercantilism, Liberalism, & Marxism
content: 👋 የቀጣዩ ክፍላችን ትኩረት የ IPE ዋና ዋና ነባር ቲዮሪዎች ናቸው! በዚህ ክፍል የመርካንቲሊዝም፣ የሊበራሊዝም እና የማርክሲዝም እይታዎችን በዝርዝር እናያለን። በርቱ👇👇 ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 📌 Overview of Classical Theoretical Perspectives Three main foundational ideologies explain how the international political economy operates: Mercantilism, Liberalism, and Marxism. 📌 1. Mercantilism / Nationalism • Origins: The oldest perspective (16th century). Friedrich List (1789–1846) is considered its intellectual father, reacting against Adam Smith's liberal ideas. • Core Principle: Demands a strong, pervasive state role in managing domestic and international trade, investment, and finance. • Trade Strategy: Focuses on achieving a balance-of-payments surplus and historical policies of autarky (economic self-sufficiency). • Modern Adaptation (Neo-Mercantilism): The state identifies strategic industries for long-term growth and supports them using subsidies, tax breaks, credit allocation, and tariff protections. 💡 Real-World Example: The rapid economic rise of East Asian economies (Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and China) relied heavily on state-guided industrial planning, known as the Developmental State Model. 📌 2. Liberalism • Origins: Rooted in classical economics (Adam Smith). • Core Principle: Promotes free-market systems, trade liberalization, and the unhindered flow of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI). • Theoretical Foundation: Comparative Advantage (David Ricardo) — countries should specialize in producing goods where they have the lowest opportunity cost and trade freely, benefiting all participating nations. 📌 The Shift: Comparative vs. Competitive Advantage In modern globalization, TNC power, government subsidies, and strategic policies have shifted the focus from static comparative advantage to created competitive advantage. • Example: Protectionism still exists in liberal regions; both the European Union and the United States heavily subsidize their commercial aircraft giants (Airbus and Boeing) to maintain a market edge. 📌 3. Marxism • Origins: Formulated by Karl Marx as a radical critique of capitalism. • Core Principle: Rejects the state as an independent actor, viewing it instead as an instrument (appendage) of the dominant capitalist class (bourgeoisie). • Current Relevance: Although command-economy systems failed with the collapse of the Soviet Union, Marxism remains a powerful analytical tool to critique capitalist flaws: - Extreme global income inequality. - Wealth concentration. - Labor exploitation and endemic child labor. - Financial speculation bubbles. 📝 Exam Hint: Make sure you can contrast these three: Mercantilism prioritizes state power/national interest; Liberalism prioritizes market efficiency/individual welfare; Marxism prioritizes class conflict/structural equality. 👉 Mercantilism (ብሔረተኝነት)፦ መንግሥት በኢኮኖሚው ውስጥ ከፍተኛ ጣልቃ-ገብነት ሊኖረው ይገባል ይላል (ምሳሌ፡ የቻይና እና የደቡብ ኮሪያ ዕድገት)። 👉 Liberalism (ሊበራሊዝም)፦ የነፃ ገበያ፣ የነፃ ንግድ እና የመንግሥት አነስተኛ ጣልቃ-ገብነትን ይደግፋል። 👉 Marxism (ማርክሲዝም)፦ ካፒታሊዝም የሀብታም እና የደሃ ልዩነትን ይፈጥራል ብሎ የሚሞግት እና የገበያ ሥርዓቱን የሚነቅፍ ንድፈ-ሐሳብ ነው።

title: 3.2. Contemporary Theories of IPE: HST, Structuralism, & Developmental State
content: 👋 ወደ የዚህ ክፍል የመጨረሻ ርዕሳችን ላይ ደርሰናል! አሁን ደግሞ ዘመናዊ የ IPE ንድፈ-ሐሳቦችን (Hegemonic Stability Theory, Structuralism, እና Developmental State Approach) በጥንቃቄ እንመርምር👇👇 ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 📌 Beyond Classical Views: Contemporary IPE Theories To explain modern global dynamics, three major contemporary theories build upon and refine the foundational perspectives. 📌 1. Hegemonic Stability Theory (HST) • Nature: A hybrid theory blending Mercantilism, Liberalism, and Marxism (heavily leaning toward Mercantilism). • Core Argument: A stable, open global economy requires a benevolent hegemon—a dominant superpower willing and able to enforce international rules, act as a lender of last resort, and serve as a consumer of last resort. • Historical Context: The global economic crisis during the Great Depression (1920s–1930s) occurred because the old hegemon (Great Britain) lost its power, while the new potential hegemon (the United States) refused to take on the leadership role. • Institutional Impact: HST explains the creation of the Bretton Woods Institutions (IMF and World Bank) post-WWII, designed under American dominance. 📌 2. Structuralism & Dependency Theory • Nature: A variant of Marxism focused on international inequality. • Prebisch-Singer Thesis: Formulated by Latin American economists Raúl Prebisch and Hans Singer. • Core Diagnosis: The global capitalist system is divided into an industrialized Center (Global North) and a primary-commodity-producing Periphery (Global South). • The Problem: Unequal exchange causes wealth to flow continuously from the periphery to the center. • Proposed Solution: Import Substitution Industrialization (ISI)—protecting domestic manufacturing using tariffs to replace imported manufactured goods. 📌 3. The Developmental State Approach • Nature: A modern variation of Mercantilism that emerged following the failure of neo-liberal paradigms in developing nations during the 1980s. • Core Concept: The state actively intervenes, guides, and drives the direction and pace of structural economic transformation. 📌 Core Pillars of a Developmental State: 1. Strong Interventionism: Strategic deployment of tax credits, subsidies, credit policies, and tariff protection (not necessarily state ownership of all businesses). 2. Efficient Bureaucracy: Highly trained, autonomous civil service to execute development plans. 3. Private Sector Synergies: Strong cooperation between the state and private businesses. 4. Performance Legitimacy: The regime earns legitimacy by delivering equitable growth, poverty reduction, and shared economic benefits. 📝 Exam Hint: Questions frequently ask about the Prebisch-Singer Thesis (Structuralism) and the core features of the Developmental State. Remember that ISI (Import Substitution) belongs to Structuralism, while export-led industrial policies belong to the Developmental State Model. 👉 Hegemonic Stability Theory (HST)፦ ዓለም አቀፍ ኢኮኖሚ ሰላማዊ እና የተረጋጋ እንዲሆን አንድ ጠንካራ መሪ ሀገር (Hegemon) ያስፈልጋል ይላል (ምሳሌ፡ ከ2ኛው የዓለም ጦርነት በኋላ የአሜሪካ ሚና)። 👉 Structuralism፦ የበለፀጉ ሀገራት (Center) እና ታዳጊ ሀገራት (Periphery) ባላቸው ያልተመጣጠነ የንግድ ግንኙነት ምክንያት ታዳጊ ሀገራት ይበዘበዛሉ ይላል። መፍትሔው ISI (የውጭ እቃዎችን በሀገር ውስጥ ምርት መተካት) ነው። 👉 Developmental State፦ መንግሥት የሀገርን ኢኮኖሚ ዕድገት በባለቤትነት ይመራል፣ ያቅዳል፣ የግል ዘርፉንም ይደግፋል (ምሳሌ፡ የኢትዮጵያና የምስራቅ እስያ የልማታዊ መንግሥት ሞዴል)። ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🙏 የዚህ ክፍል ትምህርት በዚሁ ተጠናቋል! በቀጣይ ክፍል 2 (PART 2) እንቀጥላለን። መልካም የጥናት ጊዜ ይሁንላችሁ👍!
